units.title: Start with what happened
units.description: Separate what you noticed from the story you tell about it.
units.tip: Name a specific event, date, or detail before guessing why it happened.

units.title: Make room for their side
units.description: Ask questions that uncover useful information without hiding an accusation.
units.tip: Ask one open question, then leave room for the answer.

units.title: Show you heard them
units.description: Acknowledge a stated concern while keeping your own needs visible.
units.tip: Reflect the concern they actually expressed; understanding does not require agreement.

units.title: Be kind and clear
units.description: State a limit and an available next step without making a threat.
units.tip: Say what you can or cannot do, and offer a realistic option when one exists.

units.title: Make the next step usable
units.description: Clarify actions, owners, timing, and what to do if the plan changes.
units.tip: Check who will do what and when; a proposal becomes an agreement only after both people accept.

units.title: Find a way back
units.description: Correct misunderstandings, own your part, and restart a difficult exchange.
units.tip: Name what needs repairing, correct it plainly, and invite a useful next step.

questions.context: You expected a design handoff on Friday. The file arrived on Monday.
questions.prompt: I noticed that the handoff ___.
questions.answer: arrived on Monday rather than Friday
questions.explanation: Naming the two dates gives both people a shared event to discuss.
questions.hint: Use the dates you can verify.
questions.rubric: Describe the actual arrival and the agreed date without assuming why the handoff was late.
options: arrived on Monday rather than Friday
was not treated as a priority
might be late again next time

optionFeedback.arrived on Monday rather than Friday: Naming the two dates gives both people a shared event to discuss.
optionFeedback.was not treated as a priority: That assigns a motive before you have asked what happened.
optionFeedback.might be late again next time: That predicts the future instead of describing this handoff.

questions.context: You and your roommate agreed to clear the kitchen each evening. Four plates were still in the sink this morning.
questions.prompt: This morning, I saw ___ in the sink.
questions.answer: four plates left from last night
questions.explanation: The number and timing describe the situation without deciding who cares more.
questions.hint: Focus on what was physically there.
questions.rubric: State what was in the sink and when, without judging the roommate’s priorities.
options: another sign that cleaning is not important
a problem we will probably never solve
four plates left from last night

optionFeedback.four plates left from last night: The number and timing describe the situation without deciding who cares more.
optionFeedback.another sign that cleaning is not import: That turns the plates into a judgment about your roommate.
optionFeedback.a problem we will probably never solve: That predicts failure instead of naming what you saw.

questions.context: Your friend arrived twenty minutes after the agreed time at your last two meetups.
questions.prompt: At our last two meetups, ___.
questions.answer: we started twenty minutes after the agreed time
questions.explanation: A recent pattern can be specific without becoming a claim about someone’s character.
questions.hint: Describe the two recent events, not the friendship.
questions.rubric: Describe the repeated timing difference using the two observed meetups.
options: we both need to value friendship more
we started twenty minutes after the agreed time
you seemed less interested in meeting

optionFeedback.we started twenty minutes after the agre: A recent pattern can be specific without becoming a claim about someone’s character.
optionFeedback.you seemed less interested in meeting: That interprets interest rather than describing arrival times.
optionFeedback.we both need to value friendship more: That makes a broad judgment about both people.

questions.context: A client added three pages to a draft after you approved the original outline together.
questions.prompt: The latest draft ___.
questions.answer: has three pages beyond the agreed outline
questions.explanation: Naming the added pages creates a clear starting point for discussing scope.
questions.hint: Count the change against the shared outline.
questions.rubric: Identify the specific scope change without claiming why the client made it.
options: has three pages beyond the agreed outline
shows that our agreement was not respected
will probably need a completely new contract

optionFeedback.has three pages beyond the agreed outlin: Naming the added pages creates a clear starting point for discussing scope.
optionFeedback.shows that our agreement was not respect: That assigns intent before discussing the change.
optionFeedback.will probably need a completely new cont: That jumps to a consequence before identifying the change.

questions.context: During a family call, your sibling began speaking twice before you finished explaining your plans.
questions.prompt: During that call, ___.
questions.answer: I was interrupted twice while explaining my plans
questions.explanation: You can name interruptions directly while leaving their cause open for discussion.
questions.hint: Use the observable count and moment.
questions.rubric: Describe the interruptions without claiming to know the sibling’s intention.
options: you wanted to control the conversation
we were unable to communicate at all
I was interrupted twice while explaining my plans

optionFeedback.I was interrupted twice while explaining: You can name interruptions directly while leaving their cause open for discussion.
optionFeedback.you wanted to control the conversation: That guesses at your sibling’s purpose.
optionFeedback.we were unable to communicate at all: That generalizes beyond the two interruptions.

questions.context: Two Friday handoffs from a teammate arrived the following Monday. You are opening a conversation about them.
questions.prompt: Which opening gives you a shared fact to discuss?
questions.answer: The last two Friday handoffs arrived on Monday.
questions.explanation: Specific recent events are easier to examine together than judgments about commitment.
questions.hint: Look for an event and a date.
questions.rubric: Open with the two observed handoff dates without judging the teammate’s commitment.
options: Could we avoid another disappointing handoff?
The last two Friday handoffs arrived on Monday.
I think deadlines matter more to me than to you.

optionFeedback.The last two Friday handoffs arrived on: Specific recent events are easier to examine together than judgments about commitment.
optionFeedback.I think deadlines matter more to me than: That compares attitudes rather than describing the handoffs.
optionFeedback.Could we avoid another disappointing han: That starts with an evaluation and leaves the recent facts unclear.

questions.context: The kitchen bin was full on Tuesday and Thursday, the two days your roommate had agreed to empty it.
questions.prompt: Which observation stays closest to what you know?
questions.answer: The bin was still full on Tuesday and Thursday.
questions.explanation: The two dates identify a concrete pattern without deciding its cause.
questions.hint: Choose the line you could support with the calendar.
questions.rubric: Name the two missed bin-emptying days before discussing reasons or solutions.
options: The bin was still full on Tuesday and Thursday.
It seems the cleaning schedule only matters to me.
I guess we need a stricter schedule from now on.

optionFeedback.The bin was still full on Tuesday and Th: The two dates identify a concrete pattern without deciding its cause.
optionFeedback.It seems the cleaning schedule only matt: That assumes what the schedule means to your roommate.
optionFeedback.I guess we need a stricter schedule from: That moves to a solution before describing the missed tasks.

questions.answer: We agreed on seven, and you arrived at seven twenty-five.
questions.explanation: A time difference is a fact you can discuss; the reason for it still needs a question.
questions.hint: Keep the agreed and actual times.
questions.rubric: State the timing difference without interpreting the friend’s interest or care.
options: I felt as if dinner was not important enough to you.
I would like you to try being more considerate.
We agreed on seven, and you arrived at seven twenty-five.

optionFeedback.We agreed on seven, and you arrived at s: A time difference is a fact you can discuss; the reason for it still needs a question.
optionFeedback.I felt as if dinner was not important en: That describes an interpretation of the friend’s priorities.
optionFeedback.I would like you to try being more consi: That is a broad request rather than an observation about this dinner.

questions.prompt: What is the clearest observation to open with?
questions.answer: The pricing and delivery sections are empty in this version.
questions.explanation: Naming the empty sections makes the issue clear and gives the client something concrete to address.
questions.hint: Point to the specific sections.
questions.rubric: Identify the two missing sections without labeling the client’s effort or ability.
options: I am not sure you understand what we need.
The pricing and delivery sections are empty in this version.
This proposal looks unfinished and a little careless.

optionFeedback.The pricing and delivery sections are em: Naming the empty sections makes the issue clear and gives the client something concrete to address.
optionFeedback.This proposal looks unfinished and a lit: That adds a judgment about how the proposal was prepared.
optionFeedback.I am not sure you understand what we nee: That judges understanding rather than naming the missing information.

questions.context: Your cousin borrowed your charger and agreed to return it on Sunday. It is Tuesday, and you have not received it.
questions.prompt: Which opening separates the missed agreement from a personal judgment?
questions.answer: We agreed on Sunday, and I have not received the charger yet.
questions.explanation: The agreed return day and current situation are enough to start the conversation.
questions.hint: Use the item and the missed agreement.
questions.rubric: Name the unreturned charger and agreed day without generalizing about the cousin.
options: We agreed on Sunday, and I have not received the charger yet.
You seem to forget other people’s things quite easily.
I should probably stop lending anything to family.

optionFeedback.We agreed on Sunday, and I have not rece: The agreed return day and current situation are enough to start the conversation.
optionFeedback.You seem to forget other people’s things: That turns one missing item into a character pattern.
optionFeedback.I should probably stop lending anything: That jumps to a broad rule before discussing this item.

questions.context: A work file arrived after the deadline you had agreed on.
questions.prompt: Build an opening that names the observed timing.
questions.answer: I noticed the file arrived after our agreed deadline.
questions.explanation: This names the timing difference without guessing why it happened.
questions.hint: Start with your observation, then the file and timing.
questions.rubric: Describe the missed deadline without adding a motive.

questions.context: You find last night’s dishes in the shared kitchen this morning.
questions.prompt: Build a statement about what is still there.
questions.answer: The kitchen sink still has dishes from last night.
questions.explanation: This points to a visible situation rather than judging the person responsible.
questions.hint: Start with the place, then what remains and when it is from.
questions.rubric: Describe the dishes and their timing without blaming a character trait.

questions.context: A group activity began twenty minutes later than your agreed start time.
questions.prompt: Build a description of the actual start.
questions.answer: We started twenty minutes after the time we agreed.
questions.explanation: The sentence makes the difference between the plan and the event explicit.
questions.hint: Name the delay before referring to the agreement.
questions.rubric: State the observed twenty-minute delay compared with the agreed start.

questions.context: You are reviewing the latest project brief, which has no delivery date.
questions.prompt: Build a statement about the missing detail.
questions.answer: The latest brief does not include a delivery date.
questions.explanation: Naming the missing field gives the conversation a clear subject.
questions.hint: Begin with the document, then the missing information.
questions.rubric: Identify the missing delivery date without judging the author.

questions.context: A relative interrupted twice as you explained a plan.
questions.prompt: Build an observation about that exchange.
questions.answer: I was interrupted twice while explaining my plans.
questions.explanation: This identifies what happened and when, without claiming why it happened.
questions.hint: Use the count of interruptions and the activity.
questions.rubric: Name the two interruptions without assigning an intention.

questions.context: A client’s new proposal has removed the budget section that appeared in the previous version.
questions.prompt: Write one opening sentence that names the change without guessing why it was made.
questions.answer: The budget section that was in the previous proposal is missing from this version.
questions.explanation: Comparing the two versions identifies the change without making a claim about the client’s motives.
questions.hint: Refer to the section and the two versions.
questions.rubric: Name the removed budget section and compare versions; do not accuse the client of hiding costs.

questions.context: Your roommate’s alarm rang at 6:00 on three mornings this week and woke you each time.
questions.prompt: Describe the recent pattern and its effect on you in one or two sentences.
questions.answer: Your alarm rang at six on three mornings this week, and it woke me each time.
questions.explanation: The statement separates the observed pattern from its specific effect on you.
questions.hint: Use the time, frequency, and what happened to you.
questions.rubric: Mention the six-o’clock alarm or repeated mornings and being woken; avoid assumptions about consideration or intent.

questions.context: Your friend canceled two planned walks this month on the morning of each walk.
questions.prompt: Open a conversation by describing the two cancellations.
questions.answer: Our last two walks were canceled on the morning we had planned to meet.
questions.explanation: A specific pattern makes room to ask what is happening without labeling your friend unreliable.
questions.hint: Describe the plans and when they changed.
questions.rubric: Name the two recent walks and same-day cancellations without judging the friend’s character.

questions.context: In yesterday’s team meeting, the agenda moved to a new topic before you finished presenting your update.
questions.prompt: Write an observation about the meeting, without deciding why the topic changed.
questions.answer: Yesterday, the meeting moved to the next topic before I finished my update.
questions.explanation: The observation names the sequence of events without assuming you were deliberately ignored.
questions.hint: Describe what happened before your update was finished.
questions.rubric: Identify the topic change before the update ended; do not claim someone intended to dismiss the learner.

questions.context: Your brother borrowed your car and returned it with the fuel warning light on. You had handed it over with half a tank.
questions.prompt: Describe the difference between how the car left and how it returned.
questions.answer: The car had half a tank when you borrowed it, and the fuel warning light was on when it came back.
questions.explanation: The before-and-after detail is concrete and leaves the reason open for discussion.
questions.hint: Compare the fuel level at the two moments.
questions.rubric: Mention the changed fuel level without attributing selfishness or inventing a refueling agreement.

questions.context: A teammate says the new assignment is difficult, but has not explained which part.
questions.prompt: What part of the assignment ___?
questions.answer: is proving hardest to move forward
questions.explanation: An open question helps locate the obstacle before choosing a solution.
questions.hint: Ask about the difficulty itself.
questions.rubric: Ask which part is difficult without assuming a cause or taking control.
options: did you leave until the last minute
should I simply take away from you
is proving hardest to move forward

optionFeedback.is proving hardest to move forward: An open question helps locate the obstacle before choosing a solution.
optionFeedback.did you leave until the last minute: That assumes procrastination before you know the obstacle.
optionFeedback.should I simply take away from you: That jumps to taking over rather than understanding.

questions.context: Your parent wants a large family gathering, while you were hoping for a quiet visit.
questions.prompt: What matters most to you about ___?
questions.answer: having everyone together this time
questions.explanation: Asking what matters can reveal a need that more than one plan could meet.
questions.hint: Explore the reason behind the preference.
questions.rubric: Ask about the parent’s underlying priority without judging the gathering.
options: changing the plan I had in mind
having everyone together this time
making the visit so complicated

optionFeedback.having everyone together this time: Asking what matters can reveal a need that more than one plan could meet.
optionFeedback.making the visit so complicated: That labels the parent’s preference as a problem.
optionFeedback.changing the plan I had in mind: That centers your plan before learning their reason.

questions.context: A friend became quiet during a group conversation and later said it did not feel comfortable.
questions.prompt: If you feel like sharing, ___?
questions.answer: what part of that conversation felt uncomfortable
questions.explanation: The invitation lets your friend describe their experience in their own words.
questions.hint: Leave the reason open and the invitation optional.
questions.rubric: Invite the friend’s perspective without assuming a cause or demanding disclosure.
options: what part of that conversation felt uncomfortable
was it because everyone disagreed with you
would it be easier to avoid the group

optionFeedback.what part of that conversation felt unco: The invitation lets your friend describe their experience in their own words.
optionFeedback.was it because everyone disagreed with y: That supplies an unverified explanation for the discomfort.
optionFeedback.would it be easier to avoid the group: That proposes a solution before understanding the experience.

questions.context: A client asks to move delivery earlier but has not explained what changed.
questions.prompt: Can you tell me ___?
questions.answer: what has changed about the timing you need
questions.explanation: Understanding the new timing requirement helps you explore realistic options.
questions.hint: Ask what changed before negotiating the date.
questions.rubric: Ask for the reason behind the changed timing without promising earlier delivery.
options: why the original plan is no longer good enough
whether you have considered how busy we are
what has changed about the timing you need

optionFeedback.what has changed about the timing you ne: Understanding the new timing requirement helps you explore realistic options.
optionFeedback.why the original plan is no longer good: That frames the change as criticism of the original plan.
optionFeedback.whether you have considered how busy we: That challenges the request before clarifying its purpose.

questions.context: Your roommate says the quiet-hours plan does not fit their routine.
questions.prompt: What would help me understand ___?
questions.answer: which part of your routine conflicts with the plan
questions.explanation: Learning where the schedule conflicts allows a more specific conversation about changes.
questions.hint: Ask where the schedules overlap or clash.
questions.rubric: Explore the routine conflict before changing or abandoning quiet hours.
options: whether we should stop having quiet hours
which part of your routine conflicts with the plan
why the shared rules are hard for you to follow

optionFeedback.which part of your routine conflicts wit: Learning where the schedule conflicts allows a more specific conversation about changes.
optionFeedback.why the shared rules are hard for you to: That assumes the issue is willingness to follow rules.
optionFeedback.whether we should stop having quiet hour: That moves straight to removing the agreement.

questions.context: A colleague says, “I cannot finish both requests by Friday.” You need to understand the constraint.
questions.prompt: Which question is most useful before making a plan?
questions.answer: What is involved in each request, and where is the time pressure?
questions.explanation: The question collects information about the work before choosing between options.
questions.hint: Ask for information you do not yet have.
questions.rubric: Explore task demands and time pressure without blaming organization or prematurely reassigning work.
options: What is involved in each request, and where is the time pressure?
Would better organization make both requests possible?
Should I give one request to somebody else immediately?

optionFeedback.What is involved in each request, and wh: The question collects information about the work before choosing between options.
optionFeedback.Would better organization make both requ: That suggests the cause is organization before you have learned the workload.
optionFeedback.Should I give one request to somebody el: That offers a solution before understanding the tasks.

questions.context: Your friend declines a weekend trip and says the plan does not work for them.
questions.prompt: Which reply invites their perspective without pressuring them?
questions.answer: If you want to share, what part of the plan does not work for you?
questions.explanation: An optional open question respects the refusal while allowing you to understand it.
questions.hint: Make room for an explanation without requiring one.
questions.rubric: Invite the friend to explain a constraint while respecting their choice not to join.
options: Is the cost the only reason you do not want to come?
Would you change your mind if everyone else came?
If you want to share, what part of the plan does not work for you?

optionFeedback.If you want to share, what part of the p: An optional open question respects the refusal while allowing you to understand it.
optionFeedback.Is the cost the only reason you do not w: That assumes a reason and narrows the answer before hearing it.
optionFeedback.Would you change your mind if everyone e: That uses group participation to pressure a different answer.

questions.context: Your sibling says visits have felt rushed lately.
questions.prompt: Which question helps you understand what they want more of?
questions.answer: What would make a visit feel less rushed for you?
questions.explanation: The question asks about the desired experience instead of defending the current visits.
questions.hint: Explore the experience they want.
questions.rubric: Ask what a less-rushed visit would look like without assuming a specific solution.
options: Are you saying our visits are never good enough?
What would make a visit feel less rushed for you?
Would staying an extra ten minutes solve the problem?

optionFeedback.What would make a visit feel less rushed: The question asks about the desired experience instead of defending the current visits.
optionFeedback.Would staying an extra ten minutes solve: That offers a narrow solution before learning what matters.
optionFeedback.Are you saying our visits are never good: That changes the concern into a broad accusation.

questions.context: A client says the first draft is “not quite right” but gives no example.
questions.prompt: What should you ask next?
questions.answer: Which part feels furthest from what you expected?
questions.explanation: A specific example makes vague feedback actionable without assuming the whole draft is wrong.
questions.hint: Narrow the feedback to an example.
questions.rubric: Ask the client to identify a specific mismatch without committing to a complete rewrite.
options: Which part feels furthest from what you expected?
Do you want us to begin the whole draft again?
Did you read the brief we agreed on carefully?

optionFeedback.Which part feels furthest from what you: A specific example makes vague feedback actionable without assuming the whole draft is wrong.
optionFeedback.Do you want us to begin the whole draft: That proposes a large change before identifying the mismatch.
optionFeedback.Did you read the brief we agreed on care: That challenges the client before clarifying the feedback.

questions.context: Your roommate has stopped using the shared shopping list and says it has been frustrating.
questions.prompt: Which question opens up the problem?
questions.answer: What has been frustrating about using the list?
questions.explanation: An open question can uncover a usability problem, a disagreement, or something else you had not considered.
questions.hint: Avoid building your own explanation into the question.
questions.rubric: Ask about the roommate’s experience with the list before assigning a cause.
options: Would you rather let me handle all the shopping?
Is remembering to update it the difficult part?
What has been frustrating about using the list?

optionFeedback.What has been frustrating about using th: An open question can uncover a usability problem, a disagreement, or something else you had not considered.
optionFeedback.Would you rather let me handle all the s: That proposes taking over before understanding the issue.
optionFeedback.Is remembering to update it the difficul: That offers one explanation before hearing theirs.

questions.context: A colleague says a task is stuck, but you do not know what is blocking it.
questions.prompt: Build an open question about the obstacle.
questions.answer: What is making this task difficult to move forward?
questions.explanation: This asks about the situation rather than assuming a lack of effort.
questions.hint: Start with what, then the difficulty and task.
questions.rubric: Ask about the current obstacle without blaming the colleague.

questions.context: A friend says your usual plans are not working for them anymore.
questions.prompt: Build a question about what they need from the plans.
questions.answer: What would make our plans work better for you?
questions.explanation: The question asks for the friend’s perspective without requiring agreement with your preference.
questions.hint: Ask what would improve the plans for them.
questions.rubric: Invite the friend to describe a more workable plan.

questions.context: A relative proposes changing a family tradition.
questions.prompt: Build a question that explores what matters to them.
questions.answer: What matters most to you about changing the tradition?
questions.explanation: Understanding the priority behind a proposal can help you discuss more than one solution.
questions.hint: Ask about the priority behind the change.
questions.rubric: Explore the relative’s reason for the change without judging it.

questions.context: A client is unsure about a design choice you made.
questions.prompt: Build a question that asks for a concrete concern.
questions.answer: Which part of the design concerns you the most?
questions.explanation: This gives a vague concern a more specific focus.
questions.hint: Begin by asking which part.
questions.rubric: Invite a specific concern about the design without defending the choice.

questions.context: Your roommate says the new schedule is difficult.
questions.prompt: Build an invitation to explain the scheduling problem.
questions.answer: Can you help me understand where the schedule conflicts?
questions.explanation: The question asks for context while keeping the problem open.
questions.hint: Invite understanding, then ask where the conflict occurs.
questions.rubric: Ask about the scheduling conflict without assuming the roommate refuses to cooperate.

questions.context: A teammate says they need more time for a report. You do not yet know which part is unfinished.
questions.prompt: Write an open question that helps you understand the remaining work.
questions.answer: Which parts of the report still need work, and what is making them take longer?
questions.explanation: The question asks about the work before deciding whether or how the deadline can change.
questions.hint: Ask about the remaining pieces or the obstacle.
questions.rubric: Ask an open question about unfinished report work or blockers; do not assume laziness or promise an extension.

questions.context: Your friend says they would prefer not to meet at your usual café.
questions.prompt: Invite their perspective without guessing why they want a different place.
questions.answer: What would you prefer in a place to meet this time?
questions.explanation: The question leaves room for different needs without demanding a personal explanation.
questions.hint: Ask about what would work, not what you assume is wrong.
questions.rubric: Use an open question about a suitable meeting place; avoid assuming money, dislike, or a personal problem.

questions.context: Your adult sibling has asked for less advice when they tell you about work.
questions.prompt: Ask how they would like you to respond in those conversations.
questions.answer: When you tell me about work, what kind of response would be helpful?
questions.explanation: Asking about their preferred support helps you respond to the request rather than defending your advice.
questions.hint: Ask what they want from you when sharing.
questions.rubric: Ask about the sibling’s preferred response or support without arguing that advice is necessary.

questions.context: A client says your update messages contain too much detail.
questions.prompt: Ask one question that would help you make the updates more useful.
questions.answer: Which information would you most like to see in each update?
questions.explanation: The question helps identify useful content instead of assuming the client wants no detail at all.
questions.hint: Focus on what information they need.
questions.rubric: Ask which information, format, or level of detail would help the client; do not treat the feedback as a rejection of all updates.

questions.context: Your roommate says sharing kitchen space in the evening has become stressful.
questions.prompt: Write a question that explores the specific difficulty before suggesting a new schedule.
questions.answer: What tends to happen in the kitchen that makes evenings difficult for you?
questions.explanation: The question asks for the experience behind the concern before choosing a scheduling solution.
questions.hint: Ask about the moments that create the difficulty.
questions.rubric: Invite a specific description of the evening kitchen problem without assigning blame or imposing a schedule.

questions.context: A teammate says, “I am worried that asking for help will make me look incapable.”
questions.prompt: I hear that you are worried about ___.
questions.answer: how asking for help will be seen
questions.explanation: Reflecting the stated concern shows you heard it without agreeing that help signals inability.
questions.hint: Reflect the concern they actually named.
questions.rubric: Acknowledge the teammate’s worry about how requesting help will be perceived.
options: how little progress the team is making
how asking for help will be seen
whether this job is really right for you

optionFeedback.how asking for help will be seen: Reflecting the stated concern shows you heard it without agreeing that help signals inability.
optionFeedback.whether this job is really right for you: That adds a concern the teammate did not express.
optionFeedback.how little progress the team is making: That redirects attention to a different problem.

questions.context: Your friend says the proposed restaurant is more expensive than they want to spend.
questions.prompt: It sounds like ___ matters for this plan.
questions.answer: keeping the cost comfortable for you
questions.explanation: You can recognize a spending limit without making assumptions about someone’s finances.
questions.hint: Name the stated cost concern, not their financial situation.
questions.rubric: Acknowledge the friend’s preferred spending limit without inferring financial hardship.
options: keeping the cost comfortable for you
finding the cheapest possible option
making sure everyone chooses the same thing

optionFeedback.keeping the cost comfortable for you: You can recognize a spending limit without making assumptions about someone’s finances.
optionFeedback.finding the cheapest possible option: That exaggerates a preference for a comfortable budget.
optionFeedback.making sure everyone chooses the same th: That introduces a concern the friend did not mention.

questions.context: Your sister says she felt left out when the family planned a visit without asking her.
questions.prompt: I hear that ___ was upsetting.
questions.answer: not being included in the planning
questions.explanation: Reflecting exclusion is different from assuming the person wanted every decision to go their way.
questions.hint: Focus on the missing invitation to contribute.
questions.rubric: Acknowledge feeling excluded from planning without equating it with a demand for control.
options: having to attend another family visit
not getting the visit arranged your way
not being included in the planning

optionFeedback.not being included in the planning: Reflecting exclusion is different from assuming the person wanted every decision to go their way.
optionFeedback.having to attend another family visit: That changes the concern from exclusion to attendance.
optionFeedback.not getting the visit arranged your way: That assumes she wanted control rather than inclusion.

questions.context: A client says waiting without an update made it hard to organize their own team.
questions.prompt: I can see how the lack of an update ___.
questions.answer: made planning harder for your team
questions.explanation: A specific acknowledgment connects your response to the effect the client described.
questions.hint: Reflect the practical effect they mentioned.
questions.rubric: Acknowledge the planning difficulty caused by the missing update without inventing wider consequences.
options: must have made you lose confidence in us
made planning harder for your team
means the whole project has failed

optionFeedback.made planning harder for your team: A specific acknowledgment connects your response to the effect the client described.
optionFeedback.must have made you lose confidence in us: That assumes a reaction the client did not state.

means you need a completely different living arrangement
is more upsetting to you than it would be to me
